focus: Exodus 21 begins the judgments of the Book of the Covenant with laws that limit and regulate servitude, deal with taking human life and attacks on parents, and set penalties for injuries in proportion to the harm. The chapter closes with cases about goring oxen and open pits that hold people responsible for harm they could have foreseen.

sections.title: Laws Protecting Hebrew Servants
sections.summary: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year without payment and may stay for life only by his own declaration, “I love my master, my wife, and my children” (Exodus 21:5). If the master who betrothed a daughter sold as a female servant is displeased with her, he must let her be redeemed and may not sell her to a foreign people, and if he takes another wife, he must not reduce her food, clothing, and marriage rights, or she goes out free.

sections.title: Capital Offenses Against Life and Parents
sections.summary: Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death, but the LORD appoints a place of refuge for one who killed without lying in wait, while a deliberate murderer may be taken even from His altar. Striking or cursing father or mother is a capital offense, and so is kidnapping a person, whether he has been sold or is still found in the kidnapper’s hand.

sections.title: Penalties for Injury in Proportion to the Harm
sections.summary: An assailant pays for lost time and healing, a master is punished if a servant he beats dies under his hand but not if the servant survives a day or two, and if a pregnant woman is struck and gives birth prematurely, the offender is fined when no harm follows but must give “life for life, eye for eye” (Exodus 21:23–24) when harm does follow. A master who destroys a servant’s eye or knocks out a tooth must let the servant go free for its sake.

sections.title: The Goring Ox and Its Owner
sections.summary: An ox that gores a person to death is stoned, but its owner is acquitted unless he knew that it had gored before and did not confine it. In that case the owner’s life is forfeit unless a ransom is imposed, and the same judgment applies if the ox gores a son or a daughter, but if it gores a male or female servant, the owner pays thirty shekels of silver to the servant’s master and the ox is stoned.

sections.title: Liability for a Pit and for Animals Harmed
sections.summary: A man who leaves a pit uncovered must pay for an animal that falls into it. When one ox kills another, the owners share the loss, unless the owner knew his ox tended to gore and did not confine it, in which case he must pay ox for ox.

1.brief: “Now these are the judgments which you shall set before them.” God begins the laws that will govern Israel’s life together as His people.
1.explain:
“Now these are the judgments which you shall set before them:”

The Ten Commandments state the basic law of the covenant. Now God gives “judgments,” legal rulings that apply those commands to specific cases in Israel’s life. Moses is to “set” them “before them,” placing them before the people to be known and followed. These chapters (20:22–23:33) form what 24:7 calls the Book of the Covenant.
1.notes: Many of these laws are written as case law, in the form if a man does this, then this follows. They show how God’s justice applies to the ordinary disputes of life. They were given to Israel as a nation under God, and their particular penalties belong to that covenant order.

2.brief: A Hebrew servant who is bought serves six years and goes free in the seventh without paying anything. The law limits servitude and guarantees release.
2.explain:
“If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve six years;”

The first laws concern a “Hebrew servant.” Such a person usually entered service to escape debt or poverty (Leviticus 25:39). The law limits his service to “six years.”

“and in the seventh he shall go out free and pay nothing.”

In the seventh year he goes “free.” He does not have to buy his freedom. Deuteronomy 15:13–14 adds that the master must send him away with generous provision from his flock, threshing floor, and winepress. The law limits servitude and guarantees release. These laws regulated a practice that existed in a fallen world. They did not invent or endorse it, much as the law regulated divorce because of hardness of heart (Matthew 19:8). The protections limited the power of masters and kept the servant’s dignity in view.

3.brief: If the servant came in single, he leaves single; if he came in married, his wife leaves with him. The law protects the servant’s family as it was when he entered service.
3.explain:
“If he comes in by himself, he shall go out by himself;”

A man who entered service single leaves single.

“if he comes in married, then his wife shall go out with him.”

A married man’s wife goes free with him. Service could not break up a family that existed before it began.

4.brief: If his master gave him a wife and she bore children, she and the children remain the master’s, and he goes out alone. The case recognizes the master’s prior claim on the woman given to the servant.
4.explain:
“If his master has given him a wife, and she has borne him sons or daughters,”

A harder case follows. The master may have given the servant “a wife,” probably a woman already serving in his household, and she may have had children.

“the wife and her children shall be her master’s, and he shall go out by himself.”

The woman and children remain in the master’s household, since her term of service is separate. The man goes free alone. The case recognizes the master’s prior claim on the woman given to the servant, and it leads directly to the provision in the next verses.

5.brief: If the servant plainly declares, “I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,” a different procedure follows. Permanent service is possible only by the servant’s own choice.
5.explain:
“But if the servant plainly says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,”

The servant may choose to stay. He must “plainly” declare it. His reasons are love: for his master, his wife, and his children. Permanent service is possible only by the servant’s own choice.

6.brief: The master brings him before the judges and to the door, pierces his ear with an awl, and he serves him forever. The public ceremony confirms the servant’s free decision to stay.
6.explain:
“then his master shall bring him to the judges.”

The decision is made publicly, before “the judges.” The Hebrew word here can also mean God. Either way, the choice is made formally and witnessed.

“He shall also bring him to the door, or to the doorpost, and his master shall pierce his ear with an awl;”

The master pierces the servant’s ear at “the doorpost” of the house. The mark showed that the servant had chosen to belong to that household.

“and he shall serve him forever.”

He will “serve him forever,” for the rest of his life. The public ceremony confirms the servant’s free decision to stay.
6.notes: The Hebrew word elohim usually means God but is sometimes used of judges acting on God’s behalf (compare 22:8–9). Some translations read “to God.”

7.brief: If a man sells his daughter as a female servant, she does not go out as the male servants do. The law gives her a separate set of protections.
7.explain:
“And if a man sells his daughter to be a female slave,”

A father in poverty might sell his daughter into service, usually with a view to marriage within the household.

“she shall not go out as the male slaves do.”

She does not simply leave after six years as a man would. The law gives her a separate set of protections suited to her situation.
7.notes: Deuteronomy 15:12, 17 applies the seventh-year release to Hebrew women servants as well. The rules in Exodus 21:7–11 address the special case of a daughter sold with a view to marriage.

8.brief: If she does not please the master who betrothed her to himself, he must let her be redeemed and has no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has dealt deceitfully with her. The law protects her from being cast off or sold abroad.
8.explain:
“If she does not please her master, who has betrothed her to himself, then he shall let her be redeemed.”

If the master who “betrothed her to himself” decides not to marry her, he must “let her be redeemed,” allowing her family to buy her back.

“He shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has dealt deceitfully with her.”

He may not sell her to “a foreign people.” By breaking his commitment, he “has dealt deceitfully with her.” The law protects her from being cast off or sold abroad.

9.brief: If he betroths her to his son, he must treat her as a daughter. Her position in the household is protected.
9.explain:
“And if he has betrothed her to his son, he shall deal with her according to the custom of daughters.”

If she is given to the master’s son, she must be treated “according to the custom of daughters,” with the rights of a daughter in the family. Her place in the household is protected.

10.brief: If he takes another wife, he must not reduce her food, her clothing, or her marriage rights. The law guards her from neglect.
10.explain:
“If he takes another wife, he shall not diminish her food, her clothing, and her marriage rights.”

If the man later takes another wife, he must not reduce her “food,” “clothing,” or “marriage rights.” The law guards her from neglect.
10.notes: The Hebrew word translated “marriage rights” appears only here. Most understand it as conjugal rights. Some suggest it means shelter or oil.

11.brief: If he does not provide these three things, she goes out free without paying money. A woman whose rights are denied gains her freedom.
11.explain:
“And if he does not do these three for her, then she shall go out free, without paying money.”

If he denies her any of “these three,” she goes “free, without paying money.” A woman whose rights are denied gains her freedom.

12.brief: “He who strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death.” Taking a human life deserves the most serious penalty.
12.explain:
“He who strikes a man so that he dies shall surely be put to death.”

The law turns to capital crimes. A man who kills another “shall surely be put to death.” The principle goes back to Genesis 9:6: whoever sheds man’s blood, by man his blood shall be shed, for God made man in His image. Taking a human life deserves the most serious penalty. The principle of capital punishment runs through Scripture (Genesis 9:6; Romans 13:4). The law also required at least two or three witnesses before a death sentence (Deuteronomy 17:6), guarding against error.

13.brief: If the killing was not planned, but God allowed it to happen, God will appoint a place where the killer may flee. The law distinguishes accidental killing from murder.
13.explain:
“However, if he did not lie in wait, but God delivered him into his hand,”

If the killing was not planned, and the man “did not lie in wait,” the case is different. The phrase “God delivered him into his hand” describes what we would call an accident, something no human intended.

“then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee.”

God will provide a refuge. These became the cities of refuge (Numbers 35:9–34; Deuteronomy 19:1–13). The law distinguishes accidental killing from murder.

14.brief: But one who acts with premeditation to kill his neighbor by treachery must be taken even from God’s altar to die. The altar is no refuge for a deliberate murderer.
14.explain:
“But if a man acts with premeditation against his neighbor, to kill him by treachery,”

A man who kills “with premeditation” and “by treachery” is a murderer.

“you shall take him from My altar, that he may die.”

Even if he runs to God’s “altar” for sanctuary, he must be taken from it and executed. The altar is no refuge for a deliberate murderer (compare 1 Kings 2:28–34).

15.brief: Whoever strikes his father or mother shall surely be put to death. Violence against parents is treated as a grave crime.
15.explain:
“And he who strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.”

Striking a parent is a capital crime. Violence against parents attacks the family God established and the commandment to honor them (20:12).

16.brief: Whoever kidnaps a person and sells him, or is found holding him, shall surely be put to death. Stealing a human being is a capital crime whether the person has been sold or is still in the kidnapper’s hand.
16.explain:
“He who kidnaps a man and sells him, or if he is found in his hand, shall surely be put to death.”

Kidnapping is a capital crime. It makes no difference whether the victim has been sold or is still in the kidnapper’s possession. Stealing a human being strikes at the root of the slave trade. Paul lists “kidnappers” among the lawless in 1 Timothy 1:10. The regulations about servants must never be used to defend human trafficking or treating people as property.

17.brief: Whoever curses his father or mother shall surely be put to death. Contempt for parents in words is treated as seriously as violence against them.
17.explain:
“And he who curses his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.”

Cursing a parent is as serious as striking one. To curse here means to treat with contempt or call down evil on them. Jesus quoted this law when He rebuked those who used religious excuses to neglect their parents (Matthew 15:4; Mark 7:10).

18.brief: If men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or fist so that he does not die but is confined to bed, a further case follows. The law now turns to injuries that do not kill.
18.explain:
“If men contend with each other, and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist,”

The law now turns to injuries that do not kill. Two men quarrel, and one hits the other “with a stone or with his fist.”

“and he does not die but is confined to his bed,”

The injured man survives but must stay in bed.

19.brief: If the injured man recovers enough to walk about outside with his staff, the one who struck him “shall be acquitted,” yet he must pay for the man’s lost time and see that he is thoroughly healed. The one who caused the injury bears its cost.
19.explain:
“if he rises again and walks about outside with his staff, then he who struck him shall be acquitted.”

If the injured man recovers enough to walk outside, even with “his staff,” the attacker is not charged with murder.

“He shall only pay for the loss of his time, and shall provide for him to be thoroughly healed.”

The attacker must pay for the injured man’s lost work and the cost of his full recovery. The one who caused the injury bears its cost.

20.brief: If a man beats his male or female servant with a rod so that the servant dies under his hand, he shall surely be punished. A master is accountable for a servant’s life.
20.explain:
“And if a man beats his male or female servant with a rod, so that he dies under his hand,”

A master who beats a servant to death is the subject here. The “rod” was used for discipline, but this beating kills.

“he shall surely be punished.”

The Hebrew reads literally he shall surely be avenged. A master is accountable for a servant’s life.

21.brief: If the servant survives a day or two, the master is not punished, “for he is his property.” The case reflects the limits of servitude in Israel’s ancient setting while still placing the master under the law.
21.explain:
“Notwithstanding, if he remains alive a day or two, he shall not be punished;”

If the servant lives “a day or two,” the master is not punished. One possible explanation of the distinction is that the delay suggested the master had not intended to kill. The text itself gives no finding about his intent. It states only the time condition and the reason that follows.

“for he is his property.”

The reason given is that the servant “is his property,” literally his money. The master has already suffered financial loss. The case reflects the limits of servitude in Israel’s ancient setting while still placing the master under the law. It also reveals how far that setting was from God’s design for human dignity. The New Testament later calls masters to give their servants what is just and fair, knowing that they too have a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1), and Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother (Philemon 16).
21.notes: Leviticus 25:44–46 allowed foreign servants to be bought for life. These cases show what the law permitted in Israel’s setting.

22.brief: If men fight and strike a pregnant woman so that she gives birth prematurely but no harm follows, the offender pays what the husband imposes and the judges determine. The law protects the mother and her child.
22.explain:
“If men fight, and hurt a woman with child, so that she gives birth prematurely,”

Two men fight and strike “a woman with child.” The NKJV says she “gives birth prematurely.” The Hebrew reads literally that her children come out.

“yet no harm follows,”

If the birth is early but neither mother nor child is harmed, the case is handled with a fine.

“he shall surely be punished accordingly as the woman’s husband imposes on him; and he shall pay as the judges determine.”

The husband sets the claim, and “the judges” confirm it. The law protects the mother and her child.
22.notes: Interpreters read this verse in two main ways. The NKJV reading describes a premature live birth. The harm clause in verse 23 then covers both mother and child, so the unborn child is protected as fully as the mother. Another reading takes verse 22 as a miscarriage punished by a fine and limits the harm clause in verse 23 to the mother. This study follows the NKJV reading.

23.brief: If any harm follows, the penalty is “life for life.” Read with the NKJV’s premature birth in verse 22, the harm clause covers mother and child alike, so the unborn child is protected as fully as the mother.
23.explain:
“But if any harm follows, then you shall give life for life,”

If “any harm follows,” the penalty matches the harm. If a life is lost, the penalty is “life for life.” Read with the NKJV in verse 22, the harm clause covers both mother and child.

24.brief: The penalty continues “eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.” The rule sets a limit for judges so that punishment matches the harm and does not become revenge.
24.explain:
“eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot,”

This principle is a rule for judges. Punishment must match the injury, no more and no less. It stopped endless blood feuds, where one injury led to a greater one in revenge. Jesus addresses personal revenge, not the work of courts, when He says, “But I tell you not to resist an evil person” (Matthew 5:38–42). The public duty of proportionate justice remains distinct from the private refusal to retaliate.
24.notes: The Latin name for this principle is lex talionis, the law of retaliation. Leviticus 24:19–20 and Deuteronomy 19:21 repeat it. In practice, many cases were settled by payment rather than physical penalty (compare 21:30).

25.brief: The principle extends to “burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.” Justice must be proportionate to the injury.
25.explain:
“burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.”

The list continues with “burn,” “wound,” and “stripe,” a bruise or welt. Justice must be proportionate to the injury.

26.brief: If a man strikes the eye of his male or female servant and destroys it, he must let the servant go free for the sake of the eye. The loss of an eye at a master’s hand wins the servant’s freedom.
26.explain:
“If a man strikes the eye of his male or female servant, and destroys it,”

The law returns to servants. A master who destroys a servant’s eye has done lasting harm.

“he shall let him go free for the sake of his eye.”

The servant goes “free.” The loss of an eye at a master’s hand wins the servant’s freedom. The servant’s body was not the master’s to damage.

27.brief: If he knocks out the tooth of his male or female servant, he must let the servant go free for the sake of the tooth. Even a lesser lasting injury frees the servant.
27.explain:
“And if he knocks out the tooth of his male or female servant, he shall let him go free for the sake of his tooth.”

Even a lesser injury, a lost “tooth,” frees the servant. Masters had to restrain their hands or lose their servants.

28.brief: If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox is stoned and its flesh not eaten, but the owner is acquitted. The animal that took a life is destroyed, but the owner is not blamed when he could not have known.
28.explain:
“If an ox gores a man or a woman to death, then the ox shall surely be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten;”

The ox that kills a person is “stoned,” and its meat may not be eaten. An animal that took a human life could not be used for food (compare Genesis 9:5).

“but the owner of the ox shall be acquitted.”

The owner is “acquitted.” He had no reason to know the ox was dangerous. The animal is destroyed, but the owner is not blamed when he could not have known.

29.brief: If the ox was known to gore and the owner did not confine it, and it kills someone, the ox is stoned and the owner also put to death. Knowing about a danger and ignoring it makes the owner guilty.
29.explain:
“But if the ox tended to thrust with its horn in times past, and it has been made known to his owner,”

The case changes when the owner has been warned that the ox gores.

“and he has not kept it confined, so that it has killed a man or a woman,”

If he ignores the warning and the ox kills someone, he is responsible.

“the ox shall be stoned and its owner also shall be put to death.”

Both the ox and its owner face death. Knowing about a danger and ignoring it makes the owner guilty of a life.

30.brief: If a ransom is imposed on the owner, he must pay whatever is required to redeem his life. The law allows a payment in place of the owner’s life in this case.
30.explain:
“If there is imposed on him a sum of money, then he shall pay to redeem his life, whatever is imposed on him.”

In this case the law allows a ransom. The owner may “pay to redeem his life.” His guilt was negligence, not murder, so a payment can take the place of his life.
30.notes: Numbers 35:31 forbids any ransom for the life of a murderer. The goring ox case is different because the owner did not intend to kill.

31.brief: The same judgment applies whether the ox gores a son or a daughter. Children are protected by the same law as adults.
31.explain:
“Whether it has gored a son or gored a daughter, according to this judgment it shall be done to him.”

The same rules apply when the victim is “a son” or “a daughter.” Children are protected by the same law as adults.

32.brief: If the ox gores a male or female servant, the owner pays thirty shekels of silver to the servant’s master, and the ox is stoned. A servant’s death carries its own set penalty.
32.explain:
“If the ox gores a male or female servant, he shall give to their master thirty shekels of silver, and the ox shall be stoned.”

If the victim is a servant, the owner pays “thirty shekels of silver” to the servant’s master, and the ox is still stoned.

33.brief: If a man opens or digs a pit and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, another case of responsibility follows. The law turns to harm caused by carelessness with property.
33.explain:
“And if a man opens a pit, or if a man digs a pit and does not cover it,”

A man who “opens” or “digs a pit” and leaves it uncovered creates a hazard.

“and an ox or a donkey falls in it,”

A neighbor’s animal falls in.

34.brief: The owner of the pit must make it good, paying the animal’s owner, and the dead animal becomes his. The careless party bears the loss.
34.explain:
“the owner of the pit shall make it good; he shall give money to their owner, but the dead animal shall be his.”

The man who left the pit open “shall make it good.” He pays for the animal and keeps the carcass. The careless party bears the loss.

35.brief: If one man’s ox hurts another’s so that it dies, the owners sell the live ox and divide the money, and they divide the dead ox as well. The two owners share the loss equally, in contrast to the case of a known danger in the next verse.
35.explain:
“If one man’s ox hurts another’s, so that it dies,”

When one ox kills another with no history of goring, neither owner is at fault.

“then they shall sell the live ox and divide the money from it; and the dead ox they shall also divide.”

The owners “divide” both the money from the live ox and the dead ox. The two owners share the loss equally.

36.brief: If the ox was known to gore and its owner did not confine it, he must pay ox for ox, and the dead animal becomes his. Knowing about a danger makes the owner responsible for the full loss.
36.explain:
“Or if it was known that the ox tended to thrust in time past, and its owner has not kept it confined,”

If the ox was known to be dangerous, the case changes.

“he shall surely pay ox for ox, and the dead animal shall be his own.”

The owner must “pay ox for ox” and keep the dead animal. Knowing about a danger makes the owner responsible for the full loss.
